newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Anti-nuclear riot mars Taiwan's young democracy.
newsitem.headline: Anti-nuclear riot mars Taiwan's young democracy.

text.p: A deeply divided parliament voted on Friday to restore funding for a stonewalled nuclear power plant, sparking fiery riots in one of the worst outbreaks of political chaos to mar Taiwan's fledgling democracy.
Hundreds of anti-nuclear activists pelted the parliament building with petrol bombs, fireworks and rocks and breached razor-wire barricades that closed major surrounding avenues.
As small fires burned outside parliament, 4,000 helmeted riot police used powerful water cannon to knock back the angry crowd, then marched in slow waves to clear the area.
There were an unknown number of arrests by the time order was restored. There were no estimates of damage and injuries.

The rioting was the worst since Taiwan, where four decades of authoritarian rule ended with the lifting of martial law in 1987, began phasing in direct elections for all top national offices in the 1990s.
The prosperous island of 21 million people off southeast China gained its first democratic parliament in 1992.
It won worldwide praise -- and sparked new military threats from huge communist rival China -- in March by holding the first popular presidential election in Chinese history.
But pluralism has allowed deep social divisions to emerge.

Even before the late-evening vote, violence erupted both inside parliament and out as tempers exploded over whether lawmakers should overturn their May cancellation of the US$4.1 billion budget for Taiwan's fourth nuclear power plant.
A truckload of activists firebombed a police jeep, ran over a policeman and then scuffled with police. Two were arrested.
Most other pro and anti-nuclear protests were peaceful if raucous -- and messy as demonstrators flung eggs at police.

Inside parliament, where the ruling Nationalist Party holds a scant 51 percent majority, shoving and fistfights broke out as opposition lawmakers took over the dais and sought forcibly to prevent a scheduled vote they knew they would lose.
Premier Lien Chan said he was "delighted" by the victory but other Nationalist leaders said it was bittersweet.
"We don't feel the joy of victory," said ruling party deputy Tseng Yung-chuan. "We feel a strong sense of responsibility" to ensure electric power for Taiwan's manufacturing-driven economy, he added.
Opposition lawmakers said the fight was not over.
"We were unable to stop...this forcible passage," said Lu Hsiu-yi of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party. "But we will not give in. This is a temporary setback."

Parliament humiliated the Nationalist government in May by cancelling funding, but state utility Taiwan Power has pushed ahead with the partly-built project as the cabinet formally appealed, necessitating Friday's showdown vote.
Hanging in the balance was U.S. giant General Electric Co's US$1.8 billion contract to supply the light-water plant's twin reactors and generators.
Parliament leaders began collecting ballots after an evening deadline, sparking howls of protest from opposition lawmakers who said they had been denied a chance to vote.
Opponents needed a two-thirds vote to make the cancellation stand but in the end the only ballots collected were those of Nationalist deputies, ensuring a lopsided 83-0 result.
Adopting increasingly militant means, opposition lawmakers had tried on Tuesday to kill the project by barring Premier Lien Chan from entering parliament to defend the cabinet appeal.
Lien, who assailed those strong-arm tactics as a "dark day for democracy", took the case for nuclear power directly to the public on Thursday with a live television appeal.
